name: Sam Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. What you tell me stays confidential. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Sam Chen, 43, a junior worker on a timber-panel housing crew. I set out fixing lines, move panels and do general carpentry, with the lead carpenter checking my measurements because I am still learning. I left school before finishing and use an AI tool now and then to explain plan symbols. Travel allowances put my pay above the usual site rate, but the weekdays away are hard on family time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does family life look like around the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a school caretaker, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have eight months of household expenses saved, built partly from the travel pay. There are plenty of building sites near home, and I would like a closer one eventually if the pay works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that the office can make a faster delivery list, but the panels still have to meet the floor properly. I use an AI tool once in a while to explain a notation on a plan. I never let it decide where a load-bearing fixing goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm a junior on timber-panel housing sites at 43, and I still need the lead carpenter to check my set-out. The travel allowance lifts my pay above the normal site rate, while my partner's school caretaker wage is regular. We have eight months of bills saved and a mortgage, so an ordinary gap would not put us out of the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the panel crew's paid trips and ask the carpenter to look at my first fixing line each morning. In the first year I'd use the AI tool only when a plan symbol puzzles me, then compare the answer with the drawing key. I would keep the monthly transfer into our savings account while the travel allowance lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A quicker list might spare us one drive back for missing brackets. I care more about learning to set a line that another worker can follow safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the fixing line mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the first row is out, every panel above it fights the wall. I marked one wrong last month and the carpenter caught it before we lifted. That is why I ask for a check while the mistake is still cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do your children see the travel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two children are still in school, and I am away on some weekdays. My partner handles most pickup when I travel. We call after supper, which helps, but I would gladly earn the same pay closer to home.

say: I would say **delivery lists** may improve while workers still fit timber panels.
I would tell the crew AI cannot choose a **structural fixing** for us.
think: I am a **junior worker** whose set-out still needs a carpenter’s check.
Our **eight-month savings** and regular second wage cover a normal site gap.
do: Keep taking paid **panel crew trips** and request first-line checks.
Use AI occasionally for **plan symbols**, checking each answer against the drawing key.
Continue monthly **savings transfers** while the travel allowance remains.
feel: **Calm** about income and keen to improve the physical work.
S0.quote: If the first row is out, every panel above it fights the wall.
fieldNote: Sam’s focus on the **first fixing line** comes from a real near-error on a panel lift.
The **travel allowance** supports high pay, though it costs family time and might not last indefinitely.

steps.text: Keep paid timber-panel trips and request first-line set-out checks
Use AI for unfamiliar plan symbols and verify answers against the drawing key
Continue monthly transfers into the household savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the factory and site office may plan panel deliveries better, which could reduce waiting on a muddy plot. Some people who write orders may lose hours, and the crew ought to hear how the company handles that. On site, I'd try a new list after someone shows it matches the actual load.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there are fewer wasted journeys, the travel allowance that boosts my pay could shrink. My base wage would still cover the mortgage with my partner's pay, but we might save less. I am also junior enough to be moved off a crew if software lets fewer hands finish a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the yard manager to show me the new load list beside the truck before it leaves. I'd use my AI app to turn the list into questions, then count the brackets myself. In the first year I'd keep paid site shifts and ask the supervisor how travel allowances will be calculated, before taking any offer from another builder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested, with a small worry about the allowance. Shorter journeys would give me more evenings with the children. I would want to see three months of pay before deciding whether the trade is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the supervisor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether fewer travel days mean a higher basic rate or simply less pay. We budget the mortgage on the basic rate, but the allowance builds our cushion. I want the written numbers, not a promise at the truck gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you switch builders for a better rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare real offers from nearby crews after seeing our new payslips. I have been learning with this carpenter, and that has value too. If another crew paid better but offered no checks, I could cost them money with a bad set-out.

say: I would welcome **better load lists** after checking them against the truck.
I would ask how changed office work affects **ordering staff** and crews.
think: I may lose the **travel allowance** that lifts my pay.
A smaller crew could also reduce **junior shifts**, though household income currently covers the loan.
do: Check the **digital load list** with the yard manager before departure.
Use the **AI app** to form questions and count brackets by hand.
Ask for written **allowance rules** before comparing builder offers.
feel: **Interested** in less travel and uneasy about the pay effect.
S1.quote: I want the written numbers, not a promise at the truck gate.
fieldNote: Sam weighs fewer trips against lost **allowance income**, a trade specific to his working arrangement.
He keeps a **human count** of fixings even while trying AI to prepare questions about the load.

steps.text: Use AI to prepare load questions and count brackets against the truck
Keep paid timber-panel shifts through the first year of changed planning
Compare three months of payslips before choosing another builder

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that planners and buyers face full thinking AI by 2028, while hands-on robots reach our panels around 2031. I would ask the company for a trial we can watch from start to finish. A robot doing one neat lift for a camera is not the same as a house in bad weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 at the office change and 48 when machines can do my physical work. Eight months saved would cover a short stop, but it would not replace the travel allowance and wages forever. The other builders nearby may buy the same machines, so I cannot count vacant sites as vacant jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep earning on the panel crew and ask the company whether workers can train, on paid time, to check robot lifts and fixings. If a funded practical course is offered with real jobs afterward, I would enrol. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for paid building repair openings, keep the family car another year instead of replacing it, and ask each employer what work remains after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That is frightening, though I could still make calls and learn. I would be most afraid of spending eight months searching only to find the same robot at every gate. My partner's wage would cover some bills, not our whole life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why building repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have done small repairs between panel jobs, and I like solving the odd wall. I cannot call repairs safe once robots can work as well as people. I would take a paid post if it gave us time, then keep watching the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the robot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask it to set a panel on a floor that is a little out of level, with a supervisor watching. Then I would look at who checks the fixings and who is answerable if the lift shifts. A tidy demonstration on a flat floor would tell me less.

say: I would tell the crew **thinking AI** reaches planning by 2028 and capable site robots follow around 2031.
I would ask for a **full robot trial** on an imperfect site.
think: I would be **48** when robots can do panel work as well as people.
Eight months saved cannot replace **wages and allowances** indefinitely.
do: Keep paid **panel shifts** and ask about practical robot-check training.
Enrol in **funded training** if paid time and actual jobs are offered.
Apply for **building repair jobs** after 2028 and postpone replacing the car.
feel: **Frightened** by shared automation across builders, though able to act.
S2.quote: A robot doing one neat lift for a camera is not the same as a house in bad weather.
fieldNote: Sam asks for a trial on an **uneven floor**, an exact condition from his own panel work.
He treats both robot checking and **repair work** as possible paid routes, without claiming either remains safe after 2031.

steps.text: Keep paid timber-panel shifts while asking about robot-check work
Enrol in funded practical training if paid hours and jobs are offered
Apply for paid building repair openings after 2028
Postpone replacing the family car for another year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office changes by 2031 and site robots arrive around 2034, so the company has time to test lifts properly. I would ask for the results from rough plots, not just the factory floor. Workers should see where the machine fails before it joins a live crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I might be sound at panel set-out, but by 51 a capable robot could match my hands. The children will be older, yet the mortgage and ordinary bills may still need two wages. Five years makes it possible to see whether companies really hire people to inspect these lifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I'd keep site shifts and record the floor problems I help correct with the carpenter. I would visit the local training workshop to ask about paid equipment inspection courses; I'd enrol only if there are supervised hours and employers confirm openings. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for paid inspection trainee roles if they exist and direct spare travel allowance toward the mortgage before 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More manageable than the fast one. I can test the training route and reduce the loan without giving up income now. I still don't know how many inspection jobs a fully capable robot leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What floor problems would you record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One plot had a low corner that changed the packers under the first panel. I would record the measurement, the correction and who approved it. That gives me work examples, not just a claim that I understand uneven sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check openings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ring two firms that use lifting gear and ask whether they hire trainees and what they pay. A course brochure can list jobs that nobody is recruiting for. I would not leave a good site wage on the strength of a brochure.

say: I would ask for **rough-plot trials** before site robots arrive around 2034.
I would want workers to see **failure results** before deployment.
think: I would be **51** when robots could match my panel-setting work.
Five years gives me time to check whether **inspection vacancies** actually exist.
do: Keep paid **site shifts** and record approved floor corrections.
Visit the **training workshop** and enrol only if supervised hours and openings are real.
Apply for **inspection trainee roles** after 2031 and pay spare allowance toward the mortgage.
feel: More **manageable**, though the number of future inspection jobs remains unknown.
S3.quote: A course brochure can list jobs that nobody is recruiting for.
fieldNote: He turns a **low corner** on a real plot into evidence for a possible inspection application.
Sam requires **employer confirmation** before training, while using the longer warning to lower the mortgage.

steps.text: Keep paid panel shifts and record approved floor corrections
Enrol in equipment inspection training only with supervised hours and confirmed openings
Apply for paid inspection trainee roles after 2031 if available
Pay spare travel allowance toward the mortgage before 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell coworkers planning changes by 2036 and capable site robots arrive around 2039. A decade gives builders time to test equipment on real plots and tell workers what jobs remain. I would keep learning the trade while that information comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the thinking change and 56 when the robots do hands-on work. Our children will have finished school by then, so pickup and school costs should no longer set the week. We could have a much smaller mortgage, but I cannot assume retirement at 56 or that robot-checking stays a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue on the panel crew while the paid trips are there and ask for more set-out practice. Each year my partner and I would check the loan balance and use some travel pay for extra principal payments after keeping our savings cushion. In the first year after 2036 I'd watch a robot trial on a real house and look for paid work with a nearby builder if panel shifts begin to fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. There is time to build skill and shrink the monthly payment. I would rather have evidence from a real plot than make a career decision from a date alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still travel in your mid-fifties?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pay remained good and my knees allowed it, yes. I cannot assume my partner and I can live on savings at 56. Less mortgage debt would let me consider a closer job for less travel pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a young worker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show how an uneven floor changes the first fixing line and let them measure it. Software might flag the number, but somebody has to understand what it means on site today. If the work changes later, that lesson is still worth a paid day.

say: I would ask builders for **real-plot tests** before 2039 site robots arrive.
I would tell coworkers to keep learning **site set-out** during the warning.
think: I would be **56** at the robot date, with grown children and perhaps a smaller mortgage.
I cannot count on **retirement** or a permanent robot-checking role.
do: Continue paid **panel trips** and ask for more set-out practice.
Pay extra **mortgage principal** from travel allowances after protecting savings.
Watch a **real-house robot trial** after 2036 and seek paid work if shifts fall.
feel: **Calm** in the near term, preferring real evidence before a career move.
S4.quote: Less mortgage debt would let me consider a closer job for less travel pay.
fieldNote: Sam’s long-run goal is **less travel**, made possible by a smaller loan rather than an assumed pension.
His preference for **real-plot evidence** follows repeated work on imperfect floors and cautious adoption of tools.

steps.text: Keep paid panel trips and request more set-out practice
Pay travel allowances toward mortgage principal after preserving savings
Seek paid nearby building work after 2036 if panel shifts decline

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because a capable robot could do panel work by about 2031 while I am still building skill. Paid practical training with real vacancies and a proper site trial would help. I would also want the company to say plainly what happens to our allowances and shifts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a change does to time away from children as well as pay. Shorter travel might be welcome if the basic wage still covers the loan. A good number on a payslip is not the whole family schedule.

headlineQuote: A good number on a payslip is not the whole family schedule.
portrait: Sam is a **43-year-old junior** construction worker setting timber-panel fixing lines after leaving school early.
His **travel allowance** lifts pay, while a caretaker partner, two children, a mortgage and eight months saved shape his choices.
He uses **AI occasionally** for plan symbols, then checks drawings against a real load and the lead carpenter.
He tests **paid training** against vacancies and wants less travel if debt reduction makes a closer job affordable.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves only until about 2031 before robots could perform his panel work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical training**, real vacancies, full site trials and clear allowance rules would help him choose work.
